title: Langar in hard times
hookLine: even hunted, the camps kept a shared kitchen

lines: SWEET RICE IN THE GURU'S KITCHEN.
cards: Rice cooked sweet with ghee, and a woman sharing it out to whoever sits down. That scene is in the Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad by the musicians Satta and Balwand.
The woman is Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife, and the place is the Guru's langar, the free kitchen. Generations later, the Khalsa was hunted through forests and marshes, with little flour to spare.
So what happened to that kitchen? Today: langar in hard times.

teach.b: The ballad says, in paraphrase: Mata Khivi is a good woman whose shade is thick like a leafy tree, and in the Guru's langar, rich sweet rice is shared out. A woman feeding people made it into the scripture.
The kitchen is holy ground. Then the hard century.
Tradition says that even hunted, living in forests and moving at night, the bands kept a common pot. When there was little, the little was divided.

teach.h: ANYONE AT THE FIRE WAS FED.
teach.b: And the old teaching held: anyone who came to the fire, Sikh or not, stranger or not, was fed.
Ten days ago, on the coins struck at Lahore, you heard three words, deg, tegh, fateh: the pot, the sword, victory, with the pot first. In the camps that order was a daily habit, not a slogan.
A band that couldn't protect its own village for a season could still share its bread. Tradition also says villagers who gave grain to the riders were fed from the same pot.
In the stories, the kitchen was how the Khalsa stayed a people and not just an army. Langar was never only charity, the rich feeding the poor.
In the hard century the cooks were poor too. They shared anyway: not waiting until there was plenty, but setting out what there was.

how: Gurdwaras keep langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor; Sikhs give food, money and time to keep it running.

o: a fast kept by riders in hard times
the Guru's free kitchen, open to anyone
a wedding feast for a family's guests

games.q: the pot before the sword — tap the pairs.

s: in the Khalsa motto, the sword comes first
deg, the cooking pot, comes first: deg, tegh, fateh.
the Guru Granth Sahib remembers a woman serving in the langar
the ballad of the singers praises Mata Khivi.
langar stopped in the hunted years and started again in peace
tradition says the bands kept a common pot even then.

games.q: your band is hiding in the forest with barely enough flour for itself. a stranger walks up to the fire, hungry. what does the band do?
o: send him away, there isn't enough.
feed him from the same pot, and everyone eats a little less.
games.why: tradition says anyone at the fire was fed. the cooks were poor too, and they shared anyway.

practice: Think about the food actually in your day: what's in the fridge, the snack in your bag, the lunch you're planning.

Picture one person you could share a piece of it with, a coworker, a neighbor, someone at the door, and picture handing it over. If something in you clenches, let it loosen; if you pray, let Waheguru go out with each breath.

wordCard.voice: langar, the Guru's free kitchen, kept going even when hunted: a common pot, feeding whoever came, with deg, the cooking pot, before the sword. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for langar, the Guru's free kitchen open to all.

carryVoice: Your line: share it anyway. The pot came first, even when it was nearly empty. Eight hundred eighty days now.
